title: Static friction and connected bodies
objective: Determine whether sticking is possible, choose the appropriate friction model, and solve coupled equations with consistent constraints.
why: Friction is often an unknown force within a bound, rather than a fixed number. A rope can couple two bodies while still requiring two different free-body diagrams. You will decide which contact model applies, solve the coupled equations, and use impossible support or tension values to detect failed assumptions.

sections.heading: Start with the surfaces and their relative motion
paragraphs: Friction is a tangential interaction between contacting surfaces. The normal force is the perpendicular component of their contact interaction. To choose a friction rule, first identify the two surfaces and determine whether they slide relative to each other. A block moving with a conveyor belt without slipping can have static friction even though it moves relative to the building.

This lesson uses a simplified dry-friction model. The coefficients μs and μk are dimensionless empirical inputs for a specified pair of surfaces and conditions. They are not exact universal constants of a named material. Temperature, contamination, surface wear, lubrication, deformation, and speed can change real behavior; the model is a useful approximation when its assumptions fit.

We use nonnegative coefficients with μk≤μs. The investigation permits values above one because a friction coefficient is a force ratio, not a probability. A very large or small coefficient still needs experimental justification in a real application. The chosen values here are instructional model inputs rather than measurements.

The next drag lesson studies forces that depend on velocity through a fluid. Do not combine dry-contact friction and fluid drag under one unexplained resistance term. State which interaction is present, its agent, its direction rule, and the circumstances in which its formula applies.

sections.heading: Static friction occupies a feasible interval
paragraphs: When the surfaces are not sliding, static friction can adjust to enforce their sticking constraint, up to a limit. In one tangential dimension, the signed force satisfies $-\mu_sN\leq f_s\leq\mu_sN$. Equivalently, its magnitude obeys $|f_s|\leq\mu_sN$. The expression μsN is a capacity, not necessarily the actual friction.

For a block initially at rest on a fixed level floor, with no vertical applied force, N=mg. A horizontal applied force F requires f_s=-F to maintain rest. Accept that candidate only if |F|≤μsN. A small pull therefore produces small balancing friction; with no other horizontal force, an unforced resting block needs zero friction even when its static capacity is large.

At equality, the block is at the static threshold. Rest remains an allowed state in this ideal model. An arbitrarily larger force cannot be balanced by static friction and initiates sliding. Real experiments have uncertainty and surface variation, so a measured threshold is not an exact infinitely sharp number.

Static friction can accelerate an object that remains attached to an accelerating surface. Zero relative sliding does not always mean zero acceleration in an inertial frame. In the fixed-floor problems here, sticking does imply zero horizontal acceleration. Always derive the required force from the actual constraint rather than automatically setting f_s=-F in every situation.

sections.heading: Kinetic friction follows relative velocity
paragraphs: During sliding, this model assigns magnitude μkN and a direction opposite the relative tangential velocity. In one dimension with nonzero relative velocity v_rel, $f_k=-\mu_kN\,\operatorname{sgn}(v_{\mathrm{rel}})$. If the block slides left, friction points right, even if an applied force also points right.

Adding signed forces gives $a_x=(F_x+f_k)/m$. Acceleration may oppose the current velocity, causing slowing, or may have the same direction, increasing speed. Friction direction follows the sliding velocity, not the acceleration or an isolated applied-force arrow.

A block already sliding uses the kinetic rule even if the applied force is below the maximum static capacity. When μk<μs, a pull insufficient to start a resting block can still accelerate one that is already sliding. The initial state is therefore part of the problem data, not an optional detail.

If a calculation predicts that sliding stops, end that phase at zero relative velocity. Re-test whether static friction can maintain sticking under the forces then present. Continuing one fixed kinetic-friction direction beyond the stop can produce an artificial reversal or repeated tiny oscillations in a simulation. Our investigation reports an initial acceleration and does not integrate through that event.

sections.heading: Find the normal load before the friction capacity
paragraphs: An upward component of an applied force reduces the normal load on a level surface. With maintained contact and zero vertical acceleration, $N=mg-F_y$. A downward push increases N. Use this actual normal force in both μsN and μkN; substituting mg without checking the force inventory can overestimate or underestimate friction.

For an applied force of magnitude P at angle theta above the horizontal, its components are $F_x=P\cos\theta$ and $F_y=P\sin\theta$. The candidate rest condition is $|P\cos\theta|\leq\mu_s(mg-P\sin\theta)$, together with N≥0. Keep the contact restriction separate from the tangential inequality.

If the required normal force is negative, ordinary unglued contact cannot enforce the proposed motion. For a block initially touching the floor with zero vertical velocity and Fy>mg, set the actual N to zero and calculate upward acceleration from the remaining forces. Both dry-friction capacities then vanish. A large coefficient cannot produce friction without a normal load in this model.

At Fy=mg the normal force is zero. A nonzero horizontal force cannot be balanced by this zero-capacity contact. If the horizontal force is also zero, horizontal acceleration is zero without needing any friction. The normal-contact state and the horizontal friction regime answer different questions.

sections.heading: Use an incline to expose the threshold ratio
paragraphs: For a block at rest on a straight incline at angle theta to the horizontal, gravity contributes mg sin(theta) downhill and mg cos(theta) into the surface. With no other forces, N=mg cos(theta), while static friction must act uphill with magnitude mg sin(theta).

For angles from zero to less than 90 degrees, the normal force is positive. Dividing the static inequality by mg cos(theta) gives $\tan\theta\leq\mu_s$. Thus the minimum coefficient permitting rest is tan(theta). The mass cancels because both the needed friction and its capacity scale with mass in this model.

The threshold equation does not mean static friction is at its maximum at every shallower angle. At theta=0 the needed friction is zero. As the angle increases, the ratio of required tangential force to normal load increases. The 90-degree limit is outside the maintained-contact derivation: the normal load tends to zero.

If a released block slides down the incline, the kinetic force points uphill and $a_{\mathrm{down}}=g(\sin\theta-\mu_k\cos\theta)$ while that downward sliding direction persists. A block sliding uphill instead has friction downhill. State its motion before assigning the sign, and recheck the model if it stops.

sections.heading: Separate rope geometry from tension dynamics
paragraphs: A taut inextensible rope has fixed length. For two carts on a straight track, that may enforce equal signed accelerations along the track. For two masses over a fixed pulley, one rises while the other falls. Choosing positive upward for the first mass and downward for the second lets both equations use the same signed acceleration a.

The rope-length relation is a geometric constraint; it is not a consequence of equal masses or equal tension. A moving pulley, multiple rope segments, stretch, or slack changes the relation. Draw the rope path and write how its total length depends on the body positions before assuming acceleration equality.

A common tension on both sides of a fixed pulley additionally assumes a massless rope, negligible pulley rotational inertia, and negligible pulley friction. A pulley with rotational inertia generally needs a tension difference to accelerate its rotation. We will revisit that distinction in rotational dynamics.

Flexible rope tension is nonnegative. A negative solved value means you should check signs and whether the presumed taut rope would go slack. Replacing it by its absolute value does not repair inconsistent equations. The examples specify ideal taut connections and verify positive tensions.

sections.heading: Solve each body and the combined system consistently
paragraphs: Draw a separate free-body diagram for each body. Use its own mass and all forces it receives. Then write component equations in axes consistent with the rope constraint. Unknown tension appears in both equations with the correct directions. Friction belongs only to bodies that contact a rough surface.

Adding equations often cancels internal tension and yields a shared acceleration. Once that acceleration is known, substitute into either individual equation to recover tension. Verify it in the other equation as an independent residual check. Using a whole-system mass with only one body's force inventory loses forces and generally gives a wrong answer.

For two hanging masses with +a upward on m1 and downward on m2, $T-m_1g=m_1a$ and $m_2g-T=m_2a$. Hence $a=g(m_2-m_1)/(m_1+m_2)$. A negative result is valid: the acceleration is opposite the selected positive directions. Equal masses give zero acceleration; positive masses give |a|<g.

For a table block of mass m sliding toward a pulley and a hanging mass M moving down, the equations are $T-\mu_kmg=ma$ and $Mg-T=Ma$. Their sum gives $a=(Mg-\mu_kmg)/(m+M)$. A negative result means that stated motion is slowing; it does not change the instantaneous friction sign.

sections.heading: Treat the state decision as part of the solution
paragraphs: If a coupled system starts at rest, first test whether a rest solution is feasible. For a level table block attached to a hanging mass, rest requires T=Mg and table friction of magnitude Mg. The condition is $Mg\leq\mu_smg$. Do not start by using μk if static friction can hold.

If the rest condition fails, a kinetic coefficient is needed for the sliding acceleration. Knowing only μs determines whether rest can persist, but generally does not determine the subsequent acceleration. A complete answer can therefore include a justified statement that some requested motion data are insufficient.

In the investigation, compare applied forces just below, at, and above the static capacity with zero relative velocity. Then keep all force inputs fixed and reverse the sliding velocity. Record the predicted normal load, actual friction, acceleration, and regime before revealing the force comparison.

The graph compares different initial states at fixed load and relative velocity; it is not a time trace. Its threshold discontinuity when μk<μs expresses the change of force law after onset. A table supplies equivalent numerical results, and every control works by keyboard. Save the reasoning and model limitations in lesson notes.

examples.title: Distinguish actual static friction from capacity
examples.prompt: A 4 kg block rests on a fixed level floor with μs=0.5, μk=0.3, and g=10 m/s². Compare rightward applied forces of 12, 20, and 22 N, starting separately from rest in each case.

steps.reason: The only vertical forces are normal force and weight. This computes capacity before the actual tangential force.

steps.math: F=12:\ f_s=-12\,\mathrm N,\ a=0;\qquad F=20:\ f_s=-20\,\mathrm N,\ a=0
steps.reason: Both required forces are within the static interval. Equality permits a threshold rest state.
Static friction cannot supply 22 N. Immediately after rightward sliding begins, the kinetic force has the smaller magnitude 12 N.

examples.conclusion: Static friction is 12 N or 20 N in magnitude in the first two cases, rather than always 20 N. The third case begins sliding with rightward acceleration 2.5 m/s².

examples.title: Use velocity rather than the applied force to choose friction direction
examples.prompt: A 3 kg block slides left on a level floor. A 6 N force acts rightward, μk=0.2, and g=10 m/s². Find the instantaneous horizontal acceleration with +x rightward.

steps.reason: The vertical balance fixes the normal load.
Friction opposes the leftward sliding, so it points in the same direction as the applied force.
Both received horizontal forces contribute positively. The negative velocity becomes less negative.

examples.conclusion: Acceleration is 4 m/s² rightward while the block slides left. This is slowing, not an immediate reversal. Re-evaluate static feasibility if it reaches zero speed.

examples.title: An upward pull changes both load and friction regime
examples.prompt: A 5 kg block starts at rest. An actuator applies (12,30) N in rightward and upward components. Use μs=0.5, μk=0.25, and g=10 m/s². Determine contact, friction, and initial motion.

steps.reason: The maintained-contact candidate is feasible, but its normal load is not the 50 N weight.
The required 12 N horizontal balance lies outside the static interval.
Once rightward sliding starts, use the kinetic coefficient and the reduced normal load.

steps.math: F_y=55\,\mathrm N\Rightarrow N_{\mathrm{required}}=-5\,\mathrm N\Rightarrow N=0,\ f=0
steps.reason: If the upward component were instead 55 N, even maintained contact would fail. Friction cannot compensate for a negative required normal force.

examples.conclusion: For the stated 30 N upward pull, the block stays in vertical contact but starts sliding rightward with acceleration 1.4 m/s². Increasing the upward force enough introduces a different contact-loss regime.

examples.title: Find an incline threshold without guessing friction
examples.prompt: A 6 kg block is at rest on a straight 30-degree incline, with only gravity and surface contact. Use g=10 m/s². Find the minimum static coefficient that permits rest.

steps.reason: Perpendicular acceleration is zero, and friction has no perpendicular component.
Static friction must balance the downhill component of gravity.
Divide by the positive normal load. Equality gives the ideal threshold.

examples.conclusion: The minimum coefficient is sqrt(3)/3, about 0.577. For a larger coefficient, the required friction is still 30 N; only the available capacity increases.

examples.title: Cancel an internal rope force, then recover it
examples.prompt: Cart A has mass 2 kg and cart B has mass 3 kg. A taut massless rope joins them on a frictionless level track. A is pulled rightward away from B by 15 N. Find their shared acceleration and tension.

steps.reason: Each cart has its own force equation. Rope tension has opposite directions on A and B.
Adding the two equations cancels the internal interaction, while the taut fixed-length rope justifies shared acceleration.
Recover tension from B and verify the result in A's equation. The positive tension is consistent with the rope model.

examples.conclusion: Both carts accelerate at 3 m/s² rightward, with 9 N tension. Setting tension equal to the full applied force would omit the force needed to accelerate A.

examples.title: Accept a negative signed acceleration in an ideal pulley system
examples.prompt: Two hanging masses, m1=5 kg and m2=3 kg, share an ideal fixed pulley and taut massless inextensible rope. Use g=10 m/s². Choose positive upward for m1 and downward for m2. Find signed acceleration and tension.

steps.reason: The separately chosen positive directions agree with the rope-length constraint.
The negative result says m1 accelerates downward and m2 upward, opposite the chosen positive directions.
Use the first body's equation to recover tension.
The second body's equation gives an independent consistency check.

examples.conclusion: The signed acceleration is -2.5 m/s² and the tension is 37.5 N. Negative acceleration is permissible; negative tension would have required a model audit.

examples.title: Stop a kinetic phase before deciding what happens next
examples.prompt: An 8 kg table block slides toward an ideal fixed pulley while its connected 1 kg hanging mass moves downward. Use μk=0.3, μs=0.4, and g=10 m/s². Find instantaneous acceleration and tension, then decide whether rest can persist if the motion stops.

steps.math: N=80\,\mathrm N,\quad f_k=24\,\mathrm N\;\text{away from pulley}
steps.reason: The table rope is horizontal, so weight alone sets the normal load. Friction opposes the stated sliding direction.
Positive directions are toward the pulley and downward. Negative acceleration slows the present motion.
Tension remains positive and exceeds the hanging weight because that mass accelerates upward while moving down.

steps.math: \text{At rest:}\ T=10\,\mathrm N,\quad f_{s,\mathrm{required}}=10\,\mathrm N\leq0.4(80)=32\,\mathrm N
steps.reason: Re-solve the rest state rather than retaining the kinetic force after the stop.

examples.conclusion: The motion slows with signed acceleration -14/9 m/s². When it stops, the static model can hold the system at rest. Continuing the 24 N kinetic force through zero speed would predict an unjustified reversal.

guided.title: Use the stated sliding state in two connected equations
guided.setup: A 2 kg block on a level table is joined by a taut massless inextensible rope over an ideal fixed pulley to a 1 kg hanging mass. The block currently slides toward the pulley and the hanging mass moves down. Use g=10 m/s², μk=0.2, μs=0.6, and positive axes toward the pulley and downward.
before: For the table block, N=20 N. Its sliding velocity selects kinetic friction away from the pulley.
Write T+f=2a for the table block and 10−T=a for the hanging mass.
Add the equations to find a, then substitute into either one to find T. Static capacity is not the force rule for the given moving state.

question.prompt: Find signed friction on the table block, common signed acceleration, and tension. Choose the friction rule applicable at this instant.

options.label: Use 12 N static friction because it is the largest available force
options.feedback: Static capacity is not an automatic force. These surfaces are already sliding, so the kinetic rule applies.

options.label: Use 4 N kinetic friction opposite the stated relative sliding
options.feedback: The current relative velocity determines the force law and direction. A possible rest state is a different initial condition.

options.label: Set acceleration to zero because static friction could hold a resting system
options.feedback: The prompt specifies motion, not rest. Static feasibility does not override the kinetic rule while sliding persists.

hints: The common acceleration is 2 m/s² and tension is 10-2=8 N. The kinetic rule applies because the surfaces slide.
explanation: The table block receives -4 N friction along its chosen axis. Summing both equations gives acceleration 2 m/s².
The hanging-mass equation gives T=8 N; the table equation checks 8-4=2(2). Both the tension and the common acceleration are consistent with the ideal rope.
If a separate intervention brought the system to rest, 10 N required friction would fit within the 12 N static capacity. That hypothetical rest state is distinct from the sliding state being solved.
question.answerSummary: Signed friction -4 N; shared acceleration 2 m/s²; tension 8 N; use kinetic friction opposite sliding.

guided.after: Both individual equations must hold. Tension is an internal interaction for the two-body sum, but friction and hanging weight are external. The specified initial sliding state determines which friction model is valid.

interaction.prompt: Predict normal load, signed friction, horizontal acceleration, and regime. Test the static threshold, reverse the sliding velocity at fixed force, and investigate an upward pull that changes or removes contact.

summary: Identify the contact surfaces and their relative velocity before choosing a friction rule.
Static friction is whatever the sticking constraint requires within the interval from -μsN to +μsN. Its maximum is a capacity, not an automatic force.
Equality at the static threshold permits rest in this ideal model. Above the threshold, use the kinetic rule after onset.
Kinetic friction opposes relative sliding, not necessarily the applied force or acceleration. Re-test sticking if sliding stops.
Compute normal load from the vertical or perpendicular force equation. An upward pull can reduce friction capacity or remove contact altogether.
On an otherwise unforced straight incline, the minimum static coefficient for rest is tan(theta), within the maintained-contact domain.
Rope geometry sets motion constraints. Negligible rope mass and pulley inertia/friction justify common tension only in the stated ideal setup.
Solve separate body equations, cancel internal forces consistently, recover tension, and check signs, units, and feasibility.
retrieval: A 2 kg block on a fixed level floor has μs=0.5, μk=0.3, g=10 m/s², and an applied rightward force of 8 N. Compare rest, rightward sliding, and leftward sliding. Check after working: from rest, f=-8 N and a=0; while sliding right, f=-6 N and a=1 m/s²; while sliding left, f=+6 N and a=7 m/s². The same applied force can yield different accelerations because the initial contact state differs.
